catalog_quote: 6.5.3 Tones. Almost nothing is known of the original tonal system of the Ahoms. Grierson, having indicated that there should be tones in Ahom, and that tradition is silent on the matter, stated: Moreover, in the one word, the tones of which I have been able to ascertain, they differ from those of the Khamti and Shan. ... Section 2.3 takes into a good account of the Ahom tone system. (p. 12) | 2.3 Suprasegmentals: 2.3.1 Tones: It is notable that all the branches of Tai languages, more or less, use tones (more than one). [...] Tai Ahom also used tones. (p. 27) | 2.3.2 Current tone system: The current picture of tonality in Tai Ahom supports the fact that tones are no longer in use among the Ahom speakers. new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Ahom with an empty rule and no statements. This source adds the type: tonal with phonemic tone, and confirms there is no word-stress description to record; it neither supplies nor contradicts a placement rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The grammar's whole suprasegmental section is about tone: Ahom is described as a monosyllabic tonal language with phonemic tone (five to six tones assumed for old Ahom, three heard in fieldwork, largely fallen out of use). Word stress, accent and prominence are never mentioned anywhere in the phonology chapter (the only hits for 'stress' are the gloss 'distress'); the table of contents lists no stress section in any chapter.
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress; on tone it notes that not all tones are used equally by all speakers and that the number fluctuates among speakers
new_statements.identity_note: Buragohain 2010 describes Tai Ahom as spoken today by a few old speakers and new learners in Assam (fieldwork; language otherwise confined to ritual and prayer songs, Assamese being the mother tongue). Weidert 1979 concerns the extinct Ahom of the buranji chronicles and the Ahom Lexicons, using the Latin transcription of Barua & Phukan 1964, and reconstructs its tones from Khamti, Shan and Thai. The catalog's plain 'Ahom' with an empty rule fits both; no dialect split is at issue.

new_statements.quote: [PDF p. 7, Lesson 3] Ahom is a tonal language. The meaning of a word depends on tone. A slight variation in the tone changes the meaning of a word. It is, therefore, very important to learn the vowel sound carefully from a speaker of the language. [PDF p. 62, Part 3] Ahom is a tonal language, and a word carries several meanings according to pronunciation. There is, therefore, every possibility of having ambiguity and confusion regarding the meaning of a word.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Word/Quartz PDF created 2007-09-14, text present. Both quoted passages found verbatim (whitespace-normalised) in the extracted text: quote 1 on p. 7 under the heading 'Vowel signs' (Lesson 3), immediately after the vowel-sign table and before the sign-by-sign notes; quote 2 on p. 62 as the opening of 'Part 3 : Topics in lexicon / Couplets (Reduplication)', where the tonal remark motivates the synonym-couplet device. I read pp. 3-4 (editor's alphabet/transcription table: 'Syllabic patterns', vowels; orthography only), p. 7, p. 20 (Part 2 Grammar opens with Numerals), pp. 62-63, and mapped every page's headings: Part 1 = Lessons 1-18 (script, vowel signs, vocabulary, exercises), Part 2 = Gram…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Ahom has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements; this work supplies a type statement (lexically tonal) but no stress placement, so it supports classing Ahom as a tone language with no stress statement rather than any fixed-stress reading. Nothing to agree with or contradict on placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The primer states that Ahom is a tonal language in which tone distinguishes word meanings (tones are not written in the Ahom script and are not described further); it contains no statement about word stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the Lessons (Part 1, script and vowel signs), the Grammar (Part 2, numerals through syntax) or the lexicon topics (Part 3).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only prosodic content is the two tonal-language remarks. the compilers introduction adds only orthographic notes (vowel-sign transcription), nothing on prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: The primer describes the written (literary, now unspoken) Ahom of the Assam buranji manuscripts, in Phukan's transliteration; the compilers notes Ahom is a 'dead' language, and Phukan's tonal remark refers to learning pronunciation 'from a speaker of the language' (i.e. the priestly reading tradition), not to a described living dialect.

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the open text we hold layer of Morey 2005 at the stated section and pages (6.5.3, pp. 177-178; Phukan passage p. 53). (2) The source is a 2005 Pacific Linguistics reference grammar by the leading Ahom-manuscript specialist; Ahom is extinct and attested only in a script without tone marks, so 'tonal (Southwestern Tai), tone values unrecoverable, no stress rule described' is the only defensible coding and no instrumental or fuller prosodic description can exist. (3) Of the Glottolog items not yet obtained, Duangthip 2012 (336-pp Deccan College thesis) was downloaded from the Internet Archive copy of Shodhganga and its sec. 2.3.1 restates exactly Morey's position and is silent on stress; Buragohain 2010 (JNU thesis) is open on Shodhganga but its bitstream server (port 8443) is could not be reached by automated download and has no archived copy at the Internet Archive; Morey 2010 and Weidert 1979 are low-priority

sources.citation: Duangthip, Rungkarn. 2012. Tai-Ahom and Standard Thai: a descriptive-comparative study. PhD dissertation, Deccan College Post-Graduate and Research Institute, Pune (Shodhganga hdl 10603/8154). Chapter 2 'Phonology' (pp. 44-96) and table of contents.
sources.quote: 'It is assumed that, Tai-Ahom language must have had tones when it was a spoken language, because many Tai languages like Thai have distinctive tones. But in Tai-Ahom manuscripts tones are not marked. Therefore, we have no way to study and know the tonal system.' ... (ma 'come'/'horse'/'dog' written identically) 'This proves that Tai-Ahom must have had some tones that are not marked. In our present study we have not included any analysis of Tai-Ahom tones.' No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the phonology chapter (a full-text search for stress/accent the text layer: zero hits); sec. 2.9 'Supra-segmental phonemes'
